specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

The original design compared graph snapshots. Comparison concerns the curated graph a design lives in and needs no symbol identity.

Iterating on a design asks what changed since the last reading. The first adopter asks for a comparison by Spec id, section and entry key that tells changed declaration text from changed prose, moved entries, readiness edits, relation edits and new or removed examples, and for what changed since a design pass, read against the commit that pass read (libar-platform/docs/feedback/sdp-feedback-02.md, items 30 and 31). Git shows the changed lines; this comparison shows the changed design.

Intent
actor
A reviewer or an agent starting the next design pass over a Pack, holding the commit the last pass read.
problem
A line diff of the carriers shows edits but not which Specs, entries, questions and relations changed, so each pass re-reads the whole Pack to find what moved.
outcome
Show what changed in a design between a base commit and the working tree, down to the Spec, section and keyed entry, so a reviewer reads what changed since the last pass.
Behavior
rule line 28 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:28
The design diff compares a base graph with the current graph.
rule line 29 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:29
A comparison is a catalog recipe that takes the graph sdp build wrote at the base commit as a recipe parameter and compares it with the graph the evaluation derives from the working tree, including uncommitted edits; it adds no verb or binding.
rule line 30 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:30
The base graph is input the caller holds, derived from the repository alone at the base commit; it never answers in the graph's name, and the comparison writes nothing.
rule line 31 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:31
The caller always names the base. The recipe reads no record of a design pass and keeps none, and a corpus that notes which commit a pass read keeps that note outside the graph.
rule line 32 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:32
Two graphs written by different engine versions are compared on what both carry; the result reports each side's schema version, and a difference is a diagnostic in the result, never a refusal.
rule line 33 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:33
It reports the Specs added and removed, and for a Spec present in both graphs the changes to its title, kind, altitude, stated readiness, relations, narrative and each section.
rule line 34 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:34
Inside the Design and UI sections, the open questions and other keyed sections apart from rules and flows, it compares keyed entries by key and reports each as added, removed, changed in value or moved in order.
rule line 35 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:35
Rule and flow entries match first by unchanged text, preferring the same key for repeated wording, then by retained key; remaining unkeyed base entries pair in list order, including an entry reworded while adding a key. An unmatched keyed base entry is removed, and an unmatched head entry is added. Other unkeyed entries have no identity across the two graphs and compare as part of their whole section.
rule line 36 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:36
A rule or flow with unchanged text whose key was added, removed or changed is one keyed change naming its old and new address, or none; only a text change is changed. An unchanged entry moving between rules and flows is moved; when one graph keeps no order across rules and flows, keyed entries compare by order within each list and a ruleOrder diagnostic names the Spec.
rule line 37 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:37
It reports changes to Pack membership, member order and what a Pack's order means, and to the code units, verifiers and delivery facts bound to each Spec, kept apart from the authored changes because they derive from anchors.
rule line 38 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:38
A comparison states facts about the two graphs and confers nothing. It grants no approval, raises no staleness flag, moves no readiness and never records that a pass happened.

11 unkeyed rules.

Design
diffRecipe line 42 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:42
recipe 35, the design diff, takes params.base, the graph object sdp build wrote at the base commit, an optional params.pack that limits the comparison to the Specs that are members of that Pack at either commit, and params.detail; it compares params.base with the graph binding and reads nothing else.
diffShape line 43 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:43
{ base: { schemaVersion, specs }, head: { schemaVersion, specs }, diagnostics, totals, specs: { added: [id], removed: [id], changed }, packs, bindings, leftOut }, where totals counts each list and diagnostics lists schema-version differences, parts outside the common schema, a Pack absent from both graphs, and Specs compared without order across rules and flows; base.specs and head.specs count the Specs of the comparison scope present on each side, the scope being every Spec or, with pack, the Pack's members in either graph, while the top-level specs object carries the change lists.

no citation recorded

changedSpecRow line 44 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:44
{ id, parts: [part] } in the summary and { id, parts: [{ part, change, from, to }] } with detail: true; change is added, removed, changed, moved or keyed. For keyed, from and to carry the old and new entry addresses, null meaning none; other changes carry the values on each side, a rule or flow value as { list, text }. A text change while adding a key is one changed entry.

no citation recorded

diffParts line 45 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:45
a part is title, specKind, altitude, statedReadiness, narrative, relation.<type>:<target>, a keyed entry as design.<key>, ui.<key>, question.<key>, rule.<key> or term.<term>, an unkeyed rule or flow as behavior.rules[<index>] or behavior.flows[<index>], using its head index; a removed unkeyed entry uses its base index with a (base) mark, such as behavior.rules[1] (base), so it cannot share a name with a head entry at that index; an unkeyed question list as intent.openQuestions, and any other section as its name.
movedEntry line 46 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:46
a keyed entry whose value is unchanged and whose position among the keyed entries of its section changed is moved; an entry whose value changed is changed whatever its position. For rules and flows, unchanged text with a different key takes keyed precedence, then a list change or relative order change among retained entries is moved; anonymous entries compare order within their list. Adding or removing a key alone moves no other entry.
packRows line 47 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:47
packs rows are { id, change, membersAdded, membersRemoved, reordered, orderChanged, orderBefore, orderAfter } for each Pack added, removed or changed in membership, member order or order meaning; orderBefore and orderAfter are "reading" or "priority", null on a side where the Pack is absent, and orderChanged is true when both sides hold the Pack and the two differ. An absent order reads as "reading" in every schema version; a value the head's engine does not know is outside the common schema, listed in diagnostics and not compared; that Pack's membership and member order still compare, its orderChanged is false, and the side holding the unknown value reads null.

no citation recorded

bindingRows line 48 · specs/consumers/design-diff.sdp.md:48
bindings rows are { id, implementedBy, referencedBy, verifiers, deliveryFacts }, each an { added, removed } pair of ids or fact names, kept apart from specs because they derive from anchors.

Decisions

  • spec:decisions.roadmap-priority

    A roadmap is a Pack whose manifest states order: priority; its members' authored order is the corpus's advisory priority, first entry first. order is an optional manifest field whose one lawful value is priority, and a Pack without it keeps the reading order every Pack has. Priority is preference among bodies of work and nothing more: it carries no date, no dependency, no status and no gate, and no check, recipe or page treats a place on a roadmap as permission, obligation or sequence. Everything a roadmap shows about an entry, what it still needs and what holds it, is read from the graph each time. A corpus may keep several roadmaps, and a Spec may be listed on any number of them.

18. A change proposal is addressed, based and checked before it lands

spec:consumers.intent-composition.proposal

A change proposal is addressed, based and checked before it lands

spec:consumers.intent-composition.proposalContract · storyready floor ready

Packs: pack:design-iteration-v1, pack:design-management-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 7 design entries · 2 pinned declarations · no decisions

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

The original design's patch loop made every change from a view reviewable and checked before it touched source. A patch named its target, the graph hash it was made against, a rationale, its operations and who proposed it; a CLI checked its schema and its base, applied it to a copy of the graph, ran the validators and only then rewrote the Spec files (docs/lineage/v0-design/02-system-architecture.md §2; 07-spec-studio-and-projections.md §6). The Protocol refused the patch and the codemod. A view composes scoped intent, an agent edits source as a person would, git records the edit and the same checks evaluate it. That edit model drops two things the patch loop gave: a proposed change a person can review before an agent applies it, and a guard against a proposal made against an older design.

The first adopter's agents already write proposals in that shape. A design pass returns findings that each name an entry address or a Spec section, state the gap, and propose exact text for a Spec with the entry it replaces or follows (libar-platform/design/advisors/task-pass.md), and its register tool applies a JSON patch only after checking all of it (libar-platform/design/advisors/register.md). This Spec states the reviewable half of the patch loop without the codemod. A proposal is a request that an agent applies as an ordinary edit, checked by sdp validate on a worktree before it merges. It also gives the Spec Studio's composing panel a shape to hand off.

Intent
problem
A proposed design change travels as free prose, so a reviewer cannot tell what it touches, which version of the design it read, or whether it still applies once the design has moved.
outcome
Give a proposed design change a reviewable shape: what it touches by Spec id or entry address, the commit it was read at, the change requested and why, checked on a worktree before merge.
Contract
rule line 25 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:25
A proposal is one JSON document on one schema, which a recipe takes as a parameter; a Markdown memo is a rendering of that document and never a second source of it.
rule line 26 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:26
A proposal names its scope as one or more Spec ids or entry addresses, each resolved before anything is applied: a Spec id through the reader's Spec context, an entry address through address resolution.
rule line 27 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:27
A proposal names the commit whose graph it was read against.
rule line 28 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:28
A proposal states the requested change in words an agent can apply, such as the exact text for an entry with the address it replaces or follows, a new open question with its flag, or a relation to declare or remove.
rule line 29 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:29
A proposal states its reason in one line.
rule line 30 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:30
The proposal check compares each change's scope between the proposal's base commit and the working tree through the design diff, entry by entry, and reports each change on its own row, so one changed scope never hides the state of another change; the check applies nothing and routes nothing.
rule line 31 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:31
Applying a proposal is an ordinary source edit by an agent or a person; no tool rewrites a carrier from it, and nothing is applied to a copy of the graph first.
rule line 32 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:32
A proposal carries no status, approval or verdict, and the graph records none; whether it was accepted is git history and the adopter's own record.
rule line 33 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:33
A proposal carries no proposer. Whoever hands it over is its author until it is applied, and then git authorship and co-author trailers are the record; the schema refuses the field.

{ "scope": ["<spec id or entry address>"], "request": "<words an agent can apply>", "text": "<exact entry text>", "replaces": "<entry address>", "follows": "<entry address>", "relation": { "action": "declare", "from": "<spec id>", "type": "dependsOn", "target": "<spec id>" }, "reason": "<one line>" }, with scope non-empty and request required, replaces and follows exclusive, action either declare or remove, from naming the relation's source Spec, and no other field.

proposalSchemaFile line 39 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:39
the package ships the document's JSON Schema as schemas/sdp-proposal-1.schema.json, so an agent can use it as a structured-output schema; the check recipe validates the same shape itself, and a test holds the two to the same accepted and refused samples.
checkRecipe line 40 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:40
recipe 38, the proposal check, takes params.proposal and params.base, the base graph, and returns { schemaProblems: [{ path, problem }], base, diagnostics, totals: { changes, moved, unresolved }, changes }, with the design diff's diagnostics for the Specs it compares; when the document breaks the schema or the base graph is missing it returns the problems and no change rows.
checkedScope line 41 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:41
the check resolves and compares the deduplicated union of scope, replaces, follows and relation.from, and a change row's scope reports that union, so an entry a change replaces or follows cannot move unseen.
checkRows line 42 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:42
each change row is { index, scope: [{ ref, resolvesAtHead, resolvesAtBase, moved }], moved, relationTarget }; an item's moved is true when its Spec is added or removed between the two graphs, and otherwise, for an entry address, when the entry's value is added, removed or changed, an order-only move leaving it false, or, for a whole Spec, when any of its parts changed or moved in order; the row's moved is true when any item's is; relationTarget is { ref, resolvesAtHead } for a declared relation and null otherwise.
incomparableScope line 43 · specs/consumers/intent-composition.proposal.sdp.md:43
an item outside the common schema, or an otherwise unmoved whole-Spec item whose order across rules and flows one graph does not keep, carries comparable: false and a reason in place of moved; its row carries comparable: false and a null moved unless another item moved.

specs/consumers/structural-mermaid.sdp.md

1 open question and 1 blocking question; implementation binding none, verifier binding none, and expected-outcome oracle none.

The shipped Mermaid projection draws bounded diagrams rooted at a Spec or a Pack. A Spec-rooted diagram within the bounds includes directly bound code units and test anchors; component membership and uses are read through the census and structural recipes. A view rooted at code units, grouping components by their context and layer, is now the Studio's architecture lens. Adding such a view to the shipped Mermaid root would still need a decision that narrows or replaces the projection freeze.

Intent
outcome
Draw component, membership and uses diagrams rooted at code units, once a reader needs them and the existing views do not serve it.

Open questions

  • blocking · question.namedStructuralReader line 21 · specs/consumers/structural-mermaid.sdp.md:21 · Does a reader need diagrams rooted at code units, which census tables and Spec-rooted one-hop Mermaid do not serve?Decider: ownerTrigger: a named reader with that need, plus a decision that refines spec:decisions.shipped-projections-frozen for the affected Mermaid rendering or supersedes that ruling whole
Behavior
rule.architectureLens line 26 · specs/consumers/structural-mermaid.sdp.md:26

Packs: pack:design-management-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 10 design entries · 7 pinned declarations · 1 decision

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/validation/superseded-decision-signal.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle present.

The original design checked lifecycle integrity. It flagged a superseded Spec that live Specs still depend on, and a deprecated decision still named by decidedBy (docs/lineage/v0-design/06-extraction-and-validation.md §6.3.4). A corpus may keep a replaced decision whose text still explains something a reader needs. Its supersedes edge and a shaped Spec's decidedBy edge then make a stale shaping relation visible in the graph, and this signal reads the two together.

Only decidedBy says that a ruling shapes a Spec now. A refines between decisions narrows a ruling for one case and stays true after the ruling it narrows is replaced, and a dependsOn that names a decision is not how a corpus says a ruling shapes it, so reading either would warn about relations that are not stale. When a replacement is itself replaced, the author needs the record at the end of the chain, so the warning names that record and leaves the steps between to the decision register.

Intent
problem
A Spec can stay shaped by a decision that a later decision replaced, and nothing tells its author that the ruling it rests on has moved.
outcome
Surface a live Spec that is still shaped by a decision another decision has superseded, as an informative warning.
Rule

Each world builds its graph in memory, and every probe Spec carries its kind's evidence, so only the signal moves the findings. Each probe's full id joins the probe family and its name, as probe.decision-a does. A live subject is the behavior Spec shaped in the file shaped.sdp.md, whose location table records its decidedBy row on line 7. A superseded subject is the decision decision-s, which decision-b supersedes, and a replacing subject is decision-b itself. The subject names the probe decision decision-a, and the replacing decisions are decision-b, decision-c and decision-d, which state the rung the point binds. One replacement is decision-b superseding decision-a; a chain of two adds decision-c superseding decision-b; two at once are decision-b and decision-c each superseding decision-a; a closed chain is decision-b superseding decision-a and decision-a superseding decision-b; an end and a loop at once are decision-b and decision-c each superseding decision-a, with decision-c and decision-d superseding each other. The named decisions are the ends and loop members the warnings name, full ids joined by a comma and a space in code-unit order, or nothing when no warning names any. The field and message steps read the one warning the point reports, and the message step fills the Design entry it names with that warning's ids.

rule.readsDecidedBy line 28 · specs/validation/superseded-decision-signal.sdp.md:28
The signal reads two kinds of authored edge and nothing else: decidedBy from a Spec to a decision, and supersedes between decisions. A refines, dependsOn or constrainedBy that names a superseded decision is never read, and neither is a refines between decisions.

rule.keptRecordLawful line 29 · specs/validation/superseded-decision-signal.sdp.md:29
A corpus may keep a replaced decision while its text explains something a reader still needs; keeping it is lawful, and a deleted decision leaves a dangling decidedBy that referential integrity reports and this signal does not read.

rule.onePerPair line 30 · specs/validation/superseded-decision-signal.sdp.md:30
A live Spec that names through decidedBy a decision another decision supersedes carries one warning for that pair, with the shaped Spec as its subject and the superseded decision as its related Spec; a Spec shaped by two superseded decisions carries two warnings.

spec:validation.superseded-decision-signal.live-replacement-warns · enabled, spec:validation.superseded-decision-signal.replaced-ruling-warns · enabled

rule.chainEnd line 31 · specs/validation/superseded-decision-signal.sdp.md:31
The warning names the decision at the end of each replacement chain: from the superseded decision the walk follows supersedes to the decisions that replace it, and on from each of those, and a decision it reaches that no decision supersedes is an end. Where the chain branches, the warning names every end.

spec:validation.superseded-decision-signal.branch-names-every-end · enabled, spec:validation.superseded-decision-signal.chain-end-named · enabled, spec:validation.superseded-decision-signal.end-and-loop-named · enabled, spec:validation.superseded-decision-signal.replaced-ruling-warns · enabled

rule.closedChain line 32 · specs/validation/superseded-decision-signal.sdp.md:32
The walk visits each decision once. A loop is a set of decisions the walk reaches, the superseded decision included, that supersede one another in a cycle, or one decision that supersedes itself. When the walk reaches a loop, the warning says the chain of replacements closes on itself and names each decision in a loop it reaches, and no other decision it passes through; when it also reaches an end, it names the ends as well. A loop is never an error and is never followed twice.

spec:validation.superseded-decision-signal.closed-chain-named · enabled, spec:validation.superseded-decision-signal.end-and-loop-named · enabled

rule.anyRung line 33 · specs/validation/superseded-decision-signal.sdp.md:33
The signal reads every supersedes edge whatever rung either decision states, so a replacement still below ready is named as it stands and its rung is read where the reader looks it up.

spec:validation.superseded-decision-signal.replacement-below-ready-named · enabled

rule.liveSubjectsOnly line 34 · specs/validation/superseded-decision-signal.sdp.md:34
A Spec that a resolving supersedes edge targets is not live and carries no warning for the decisions it names. A decision that supersedes another stays live until it is itself superseded, so its own decidedBy relations warn as any live Spec's do, even when the walk from the decision it names reaches it.

read the resolving, declared supersedes edges whose source and target are both decision Specs, and index each by its target; from the superseded decision, visit each decision reachable along those edges from target to source once; an end is a reached decision other than the start that no such edge targets; a loop member is a reached decision, the start included, in a strongly connected component of two or more decisions or with an edge to itself; ends and loop members are collected apart.

Decisions

  • spec:decisions.planning-truths-placement

    Each planning-truth type lives in its ruled home. Work-item dependency truth rides dependsOn edges, with independence as absence of the edge and scheduling phrases never authored. Decision gates live on decision-kind Specs, linked by decidedBy. Do-not-reopen rows split by what they carry: a tradeoff refusal becomes a decision-kind Spec, which a later decision that supersedes it replaces whole and a later decision that refines it narrows for one case, either under the ADR three-part test; a row that restates a behavior guarantee already homed on a carrying Spec stays on that Spec and changes by ordinary Spec revision; a hold stays a blocking open question on its own Spec and is never minted as a decision. A lawful non-decision stays in the plan record as evidence. A deferral carries its re-entry trigger in the trigger field of its own blocking open question, and declares dependsOn separately when a true precondition exists. Exclusive ownership is one Spec identity per deliverable with consumers depending on it. Selection-pressure heuristics are advisory only, carried as behavior rules on the graph-first planning Spec or in recipes. Session law splits separately, across behavior rules on the graph-first planning Spec, the delivery-session on-ramp's handoff rule, and the plan file. The briefs index shape is retired as a carrier of law.

spec:validation.architecture-constraints

Declared architecture rules are checked against anchored structure

specs/validation/architecture-constraints.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

The original design gave architecture a validation tier of its own. Its rules said that only adapter components depend on external systems, that domain code imports no infrastructure and that layers depend in one direction; dependency-cruiser, architecture tests and lint rules ran them, and their findings joined the one report (docs/lineage/v0-design/06-extraction-and-validation.md §6.4). Since the architectural annotation decision, the data those rules read is in the graph with no inference: a component anchor states its layer and its context, and uses and memberOf edges are anchored. The same decision keeps the check out of the Protocol. A negative architecture constraint stays declared intent in a Spec, and a corpus that wants it enforced checks its declared uses, layer and context in its own gate.

The first adopter checks that a component in its platform context has no uses edge to a component in another context, resolving each end through memberOf. Architecture crossings, recipe 32, reports differences in context or layer and refuses nothing. The architectural annotation decision keeps architecture checks in the corpus's own gate, and the Protocol supplies the reusable graph walk.

The walk returns the edges a rule forbids as corpus findings, so one body answers a reader through sdp q and fails a gate when the corpus names it as a rules file; the first adopter's isolation check becomes the walk named by sdp validate --rules with the isolated context platform, and none of its own code. An edge the walk cannot decide, because a component states no layer or context or an end belongs to no component, is listed apart: a breach the anchors cannot show is a curation gap, not a finding.

Intent
problem
A corpus that states an architecture rule in a Spec cannot have it checked by the Protocol, so each adopter writes the same walk over uses, memberOf, layer and context in its own gate.
outcome
Check a corpus's declared architecture rules, such as a forbidden uses direction or context isolation, against the layers, contexts and uses its anchors state.

Design view

Requirement drawing

Decisions

  • spec:decisions.architectural-annotation

    Architectural significance is annotated on the anchor of the unit that realizes it. A code anchor may carry role, the architectural pattern the unit plays; a component: anchor may additionally carry layer, one of edge, application, domain, adapter, or infrastructure, and context, its bounded context. The component: anchor is anchored architecture: it is the declared component, and there is no separate architecture file, because the anchor sits where the component is realized. It is not the original design's declared Component that could exist before code; an unrealized component lives in Specs and never as an invented CodeNode. A role is a free, corpus-owned vocabulary whose taxonomy the census renders with counts from the graph; service, decider, projection, read-model, codec, contract, barrel, and utility are the lineage set, not a closed list. layer is a closed set, and a value outside it is an envelope error; layer or context on a non-component anchor is an envelope error. All three attributes are optional, and omission is lawful.

specs/validation/corpus-rules.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle present.

The original design let a team add its own rules beside the built-in validators, each with an id, a severity and the whole graph query API, run in the same pass and reported in the same output (docs/lineage/v0-design/06-extraction-and-validation.md §6.5). The Protocol has two check families, conformance and honesty, and every validator belongs to one of them. The architectural annotation decision sends a corpus's own rules to the corpus's own gate.

The first adopter's gate runs sdp validate and parses its summary line, then checks its own context isolation, entry addresses, dependency cycles, question keys, prose mentions, cited laws and Pack pages. It also parses carrier frontmatter to read kind, readiness and relations, a second read model that a graph-based corpus-rule runner would remove.

A rules file holds the body sdp q evaluates, so a rule tried through sdp q runs unchanged under sdp validate, and a catalog recipe whose answer carries findings, such as the architecture walk, is a rules file as shipped. A rules file that needs a shipped recipe's answer calls it through recipes and keeps no copy of its code. The runner reads only the answer's findings, so the recipe keeps the rest of its answer for a reader. Corpus findings print after the Protocol's and are tallied on a line of their own, so a gate that reads the Protocol's summary line reads it unchanged; any error, the Protocol's or the corpus's, exits 1, and the two lines say which. Each rules file receives its own copy of what it reads, so a careless rule cannot change another rule's input and the order of the files changes only the order of the output. Its parameters are its own too: a catalog recipe answers a parameter name it does not take with that name and no findings, so parameters shared by every file would fail the walk on the names another file reads.

Intent
problem
A corpus with rules of its own checks them off the one validation path, reading the carriers a second way and reporting in a form no Protocol surface reads.
outcome
Let a corpus author its own graph rules and have their findings join the one validation report, so no corpus re-parses its carriers to check itself.

Design
rulesFlag line 56 · specs/validation/corpus-rules.sdp.md:56
sdp validate [root] [--exclude PATH]... [--check-clean | --watch] [--rules PATH [--params JSON | --params @PATH | --params KEY=@PATH]...]...; --rules and --params are options of validate alone, a --params before the first --rules is refused, one file named twice is refused, including through a symlink, and each PATH resolves from the working directory, as a --params @PATH file does. Diagnostics retain the path the operator named.

no citation recorded

paramsFlag line 57 · specs/validation/corpus-rules.sdp.md:57
--params on validate takes the three forms of sdp q --params with the same refusals, before the graph derives; each --params belongs to the nearest --rules before it in the argument list, whatever other options stand between them; one file's parameters merge as sdp q merges them, a key given twice for one file is refused, two files may each take the same key, and a file with no --params after it receives {}.

no citation recorded

rulesFile line 58 · specs/validation/corpus-rules.sdp.md:58
a rules file is UTF-8 text holding one plain JavaScript async function body, the form sdp q evaluates, with the bindings g, graph, report, params and recipes; the runner reads the text and never imports it as a module, so no file extension is required and a catalog recipe file under dist/recipes/ is a lawful rules file.
ruleAnswer line 59 · specs/validation/corpus-rules.sdp.md:59
{ findings: [] }: the body returns an object whose findings is an array, possibly empty; the runner reads findings and nothing else, so the answer's other keys stay the body's own data and are never printed.

no citation recorded

ruleFinding line 60 · specs/validation/corpus-rules.sdp.md:60
{ validatorId, subjectId, severity, message, relatedId?, path?, file?, line? }, where validatorId is the rule id, one token matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$, so it never reads as a Protocol validator id; subjectId and message are non-empty strings; severity is "error" or "warning"; relatedId and path are strings; file is a non-empty root-relative POSIX path, with absolute paths, backslashes and traversal above the root refused, and line a positive integer that requires file; the runner ignores a finding's other keys.

Design view

Requirement drawing

Decisions

  • spec:decisions.architectural-annotation

    Architectural significance is annotated on the anchor of the unit that realizes it. A code anchor may carry role, the architectural pattern the unit plays; a component: anchor may additionally carry layer, one of edge, application, domain, adapter, or infrastructure, and context, its bounded context. The component: anchor is anchored architecture: it is the declared component, and there is no separate architecture file, because the anchor sits where the component is realized. It is not the original design's declared Component that could exist before code; an unrealized component lives in Specs and never as an invented CodeNode. A role is a free, corpus-owned vocabulary whose taxonomy the census renders with counts from the graph; service, decider, projection, read-model, codec, contract, barrel, and utility are the lineage set, not a closed list. layer is a closed set, and a value outside it is an envelope error; layer or context on a non-component anchor is an envelope error. All three attributes are optional, and omission is lawful.

24. CI run records are joined to verifiers in a view

spec:observation.run-evidence

CI run records are joined to verifiers in a view

spec:observation.run-evidenceUse Case / Behavior · featureready floor ready

Packs: pack:design-management-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1, pack:spec-studio-v1

Design: 7 design entries · 5 pinned declarations · 1 decision

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/observation/run-evidence.sdp.md

1 open question and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle present.

The original design put test reports in the graph and used passing runs to mark verification. The Protocol keeps run verdicts in CI. A resolving verifier binding confers has-verifier; showing a recorded run beside that binding confers no delivery fact. Runtime observation against a measurable target is a separate concern carried by the runtime overlay.

An adopter that keeps CI run reports needs to read them beside verifier bindings as a separately named input. Recipe 45 reads them, and the Studio admits them as one of its two named inputs. The view identifies each run by its own fields and its commit, and distinguishes evidence from a test file from a verdict for one anchored verifier. Test reporters write a test's file as an absolute path or a path from the directory they ran in, so the join reads a path's end as well as the whole path. The freshness question records what remains unsettled about comparing a run with the source being read.

Intent
problem
A reader who wants to know whether a bound verifier passed has to leave the Protocol's views for CI, and an adopter that keeps run records has no view that shows them beside the binding without mistaking them for a delivery fact.
outcome
Show a verifier's recorded runs beside its binding in a view, labelled as external input with its commit, while the graph keeps recording only that the binding exists.

Open questions

  • non-blocking · question.freshness line 28 · specs/observation/run-evidence.sdp.md:28 · How does a view say a run is stale: by its commit against the commit being read, or by whether the bound files changed between the two?Decider: ownerProvisional: Display the run and source commit identifiers when they differ, as the differing-commit rule requires; whether freshness also follows changes to bound files remains open.
Behavior
rule.graphUntouched line 33 · specs/observation/run-evidence.sdp.md:33
Run records are an input a view reads beside the graph, named by the caller; the graph never holds them, and no node, edge or delivery fact derives from them.

spec:observation.run-evidence.absolute-path-joins · enabled, spec:observation.run-evidence.unanchored-file-unjoined · enabled

rule.fileGrain line 34 · specs/observation/run-evidence.sdp.md:34
A run record joins every verifier whose test anchor sits in the test file the record names, because the file is the binding grain of both anchor forms; each test name in the record shows as a row under that verifier. The join is at file grain: a result is evidence from the verifier's file, never the result of that verifier, because a file may hold several suites and a filtered run may exercise only one.

spec:observation.run-evidence.absolute-path-joins · enabled

rule.ctrfInput line 35 · specs/observation/run-evidence.sdp.md:35
The Protocol reads run records in the Common Test Report Format, CTRF, an open JSON schema with reporters for the common test runners, passed to a view as a recipe parameter. A record joins only when its reporter fills CTRF's optional filePath field, and an adopter with records of another shape maps them into CTRF itself.

spec:observation.run-evidence.absolute-path-joins · enabled

rule.pathNormalization line 36 · specs/observation/run-evidence.sdp.md:36
A record's file path joins a test anchor's file when, with each backslash written as a slash and a leading ./ removed, it equals that file or ends with a slash followed by that file; when several anchored files match, the longest joins.

spec:observation.run-evidence.absolute-path-joins · enabled

rule.unjoinedReported line 37 · specs/observation/run-evidence.sdp.md:37
A record that names no file path, or a file that holds no test anchor, is reported as unjoined with its reason, never dropped, and an input that is not a CTRF report is reported with its problem while the other inputs still join.

spec:observation.run-evidence.unanchored-file-unjoined · enabled

rule.commitField line 38 · specs/observation/run-evidence.sdp.md:38
A run's commit is CTRF's results.environment.commit, and a run without one reads not recorded; given the commit being read, the recipe says for each run whether its commit is that commit, and never says the run is fresh or stale.

no example exercises it

rule line 39 · specs/observation/run-evidence.sdp.md:39
A view shows each run beside the verifiers anchored in its file, with its result, its commit and the input it came from, labelled as external run evidence from that file and never as has-verifier, implemented or a pass verdict for one verifier.
rule line 40 · specs/observation/run-evidence.sdp.md:40
A run whose commit differs from the commit being read shows both commits, so a reader sees how old it is.
rule.studioInput line 41 · specs/observation/run-evidence.sdp.md:41
The Design Review stays a function of the graph alone and shows no run; run evidence appears only in a view that explicitly admits records as external input: recipe 45, and the Studio built with run records, which shows them on its runs page, in its tests lens and on the Spec pages of the Specs their files verify.

runsRecipe line 44 · specs/observation/run-evidence.sdp.md:44
recipe 45, run evidence, takes params.runs, one CTRF report or a list of them in input order, required; params.commit, the commit being read, optional; and params.spec, a Spec id, optional, which keeps only the files whose test anchors verify that Spec directly or through an enabled example. It returns { inputs, diagnostics, totals, files, unjoined }, and { diagnostics } alone when params.runs is missing or holds no report it can read.
ctrfFields line 45 · specs/observation/run-evidence.sdp.md:45
the recipe reads reportFormat and specVersion; results.tool.name and version; results.summary with tests, passed, failed, skipped, pending, other, start and stop; results.environment with commit, branchName, buildName and buildNumber; and per test name, status, duration, filePath and suite; it reads no other field. A readable CTRF report has reportFormat: "CTRF" and a specVersion, as the CTRF schema requires; a report missing either produces a run diagnostic and contributes no run rows.
